blurb:
Zombie animals are real. Meatball tells the true story of five animals whose bodies get driven by something else: the zombie-ant fungus and its death grip, the emerald wasp that walks a cockroach on a leash, the hairworm that makes crickets jump into water, the snail with throbbing striped eyes, and the parasite that makes rats like cats. One of them is has infected somewhere between a quarter and a third of all people. It's at the end.

beats.say: Zombies are real. Five animals on Earth get taken over by something that drives their body for them. And one of those things might be inside you right now. That one's at the end.
This ant is about to climb to its death.
This cockroach is about to get walked like a dog.
I'm Meatball. I narrate nature, and nature keeps trying to eat me. Today: real zombie animals.
First, the zombie ant. Deep in a rainforest, a carpenter ant walks past a tiny fungus spore. The spore sticks to it. That's it. That's the whole mistake.
The fungus is called Ophiocordyceps. It gets through the ant's armor and starts growing inside its body.
Over the next week or two it spreads everywhere. When scientists scanned infected ants, they found fungus cells wrapped around the ant's muscles, like a net.
And here's the creepy part. The fungus mostly leaves the brain alone. The ant is still in there. It's just not driving.
Then the ant leaves its nest. It climbs a plant, stops about a ruler's length above the forest floor, and clamps its jaws onto a vein under a leaf. Scientists call it the death grip.
In one study, the ants bit down around the middle of the day. Like it was scheduled.
Quick thing. If watching a meatball narrate things that would happily eat him is your idea of fun, subscribing genuinely keeps me off the menu. A ghost told me that.
Back to the ant. It dies right there, locked on. And then a stalk grows out of the back of its head.
From up there, the stalk rains spores down onto the trail below. Right where the next ant walks.
And this is old. Scientists found the same bite scars on a fossil leaf about forty eight million years old. Ants were getting zombified before there were any people to be scared of it.
Honestly? As a food item, I relate to the ant. Something else decides your whole day, and then it's over.
Number two is a wasp. The emerald cockroach wasp. Shiny, green, and smaller than a paper clip.
beats.chapter: The wasp that walks a cockroach

beats.say: Its target is a cockroach. A cockroach that's bigger than it is.
The first sting goes into the chest. The roach's front legs stop working for a couple of minutes.
The second sting goes into the head. Into the brain. The wasp actually feels around with its stinger for the right spot.
Now here's the thing. The roach isn't paralyzed. It can walk just fine. It just doesn't want to escape anymore.
So the wasp bites off part of each antenna, grabs what's left, and leads the cockroach to its burrow. Like a dog on a leash.
And the cockroach just follows. It walks into the burrow by itself.
The wasp lays one egg on the roach's leg, seals the door with pebbles, and flies off.
When the egg hatches, the baby wasp eats the cockroach. From the inside. And the roach stays alive for most of it.
Weeks later, a brand new wasp climbs out of the cockroach. The cockroach does not.
If that one got you, hit like. I need to know you're as upset as I am.
Number three. A cricket walks to the edge of a pond, and jumps in.
beats.chapter: The cricket that jumps into water

beats.say: Crickets are terrible swimmers. They normally stay away from water. This one jumped anyway.
Because there's a worm inside it. A hairworm. It grew up inside the cricket, feeding on it from the inside, coiled up in there the whole time.
A hairworm can only finish growing up in water. And in experiments, infected crickets jumped into water far more often than healthy ones.
The second the cricket hits the water, the worm slides out. It can be several times longer than the cricket it came out of.
People find these worms in swimming pools, dog bowls and toilets. They look like a hair that's moving. They're harmless to people. Have a lovely evening.
Number four is the one with the dancing eyes.
This is an amber snail. Snails are normally slow, careful, and big fans of shade.
But this one has a flatworm inside it called Leucochloridium. It fills the snail's eye stalks with fat, striped, throbbing sacs.
They pulse. Green, banded, wiggling. To a bird, that looks a lot like a juicy caterpillar.
And infected snails tend to sit higher up, out in the open, in the light. Exactly where birds are looking.
A bird pecks off the eye stalk. The worm grows up inside the bird. The bird poops out the worm's eggs. Another snail eats the poop. And round it goes.
The snail can even grow its eye stalk back. Which, honestly, makes it worse.
Your turn. Which of these would make the scariest Halloween costume? Tell me in the comments. Wrong answers welcome. The best one gets read out next episode.
Okay. I promised you one of these might be inside you right now. Here it is.
beats.chapter: The one that might be in you

beats.say: It's a tiny parasite called Toxoplasma. It can live in almost any warm-blooded animal. Rats, birds, sheep. People.
But it can only finish its life cycle in one place. The gut of a cat.
So it needs to get from the rat into the cat. And here's what scientists found.
Healthy rats stay away from places that smell like cat pee. Smart rats. Infected rats didn't. In one famous experiment, they seemed to prefer it.
And a rat that likes the smell of cats is a rat that ends up inside a cat. Which is exactly where the parasite wanted to go.

Now, people. Scientists estimate that somewhere between a quarter and a third of all people on Earth have caught Toxoplasma at some point. Usually from undercooked meat, unwashed veggies, or a cat's litter box.
Undercooked meat. For the record, I am fully cooked.
For almost everyone, it's harmless. Your immune system keeps it asleep, and you never notice. Scientists still argue about whether it changes people at all, and most say: not in any way you'd notice.
The big exceptions are pregnancy and people with very weak immune systems. That's why doctors tell pregnant people to let somebody else clean the litter box.
So no, you are not a zombie. Probably. But if you've ever had a sudden, powerful urge to get a cat, I'm just saying.
That's five puppet masters. A fungus, a wasp, a worm, a flatworm and a microbe. Two of them don't even have a brain. And every one of them can drive.
